sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
Mismatches between the transistors inside an op-amp make its output non-zero even when the inputs are tied together. We model this as a small DC source, the **input offset voltage** \(V_{os}\), in series with one input of an otherwise ideal op-amp. Its sign and size vary randomly from part to part.

Open loop, even a millivolt times a huge \(A_0\) slams the output into a rail. In a feedback circuit, \(V_{os}\) is amplified by the **noise gain** \(1/f = 1 + R_2/R_1\), which is the non-inverting gain, regardless of whether the signal is applied to the inverting or the non-inverting input. Offset is a DC error, unlike noise, which is random AC.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Open loop: \(V_o = A_0 V_{os}\) (until it saturates).
Closed loop (either configuration, signal grounded):
\[ V_o = V_{os}\left(1 + \frac{R_2}{R_1}\right) \]
Offset drift: \(\Delta V_{os} = \dfrac{dV_{os}}{dT}\,\Delta T\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
An inverting amplifier with \(R_1 = 1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(R_2 = 49\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) (signal gain \(-49\)) uses an op-amp with \(V_{os} = 1.5\ \mathrm{mV}\). With the input grounded:
\[ V_o = 1.5\ \mathrm{mV}\times(1 + 49) = 75\ \mathrm{mV} \]
Not \(-49\times1.5\ \mathrm{mV}\): the offset sees the noise gain of 50.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Using the inverting signal gain \(-R_2/R_1\) for the offset.
- Treating offset as noise.
- Assuming the sign is known; datasheets give a maximum magnitude.
- Forgetting offset changes with temperature.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Offset, bias currents and noise together set the smallest signal an amplifier can handle accurately. Datasheets specify all three, usually with maximum and temperature-drift values. A quick worst-case estimate multiplies the maximum datasheet offset by the noise gain.
